Single continuous take, 8 seconds, real time. No cuts, no fades, no speed ramps.

OPTICS
84 degree diagonal field of view, wide lens character, deep edge-to-edge focus,
straight lines rectilinear, wide spatial context visible to the frame edges. Both
seated people stay small and distant in frame throughout; the camera never gets
closer to them.

CAMERA
The camera is locked off on sticks and does not move at all: no pan, no tilt, no
push, no drift, no reframe, no handheld float, no zoom. The frame at the last
second is the same frame as at the first second.

ACTION TIMING
Continuous throughout, no beats and no events. The fire burns with a steady low
flame that flickers irregularly and throws a soft pulsing warm glow on the ground
immediately around it. Pale grey smoke rises from the fire in one unbroken column
and leans up and toward frame-left, thinning as it climbs. The grass across the
whole field moves in one slow broad wave travelling from frame-right to
frame-left, blades bending together and springing back. Both seated people
breathe: shoulders rising and settling slowly, out of step with each other. The
loose hem of the pale chapan lifts and settles at the same rhythm as the grass,
its cloth catching a faint cold sheen from the sky as it moves. A few strands of
the dark-clad one's hair lift and fall. The horses and the figures by the fire
hold their positions and are not asked to move.

PHYSICS
The smoke has real buoyancy and drifts with the same wind that moves the grass,
never against it. The flame has weight at its base and flickers at its tip. The
grass carries the wind as one continuous travelling wave across the field, never
as independent trembling blades. The heavy chapan cloth follows the body with a
delay and falls back under its own weight.

LIGHTING
Blue hour after sunset. The sky is the brightest thing in frame and the field is
two stops under it. The only warm source is the campfire, and its light reaches
no further than a few metres around it. Neither seated person is lit by the fire;
both read as dark shapes against the field, the pale chapan separating from the
ground only by its own faint sheen. Neutral white balance, no artificial lift in
the shadows, no second light source anywhere.

AUDIO
SFX only. No music, no score, no instruments of any kind.
Foreground, closest and loudest: a low steady steppe wind moving over dry grass,
broad and continuous for the whole take, never gusting hard.
Background, far away and quiet, coming only from the camp at frame-left: the soft
irregular crackle and settle of the campfire, and a few men talking together in
Dari, the Afghan Persian language — a calm, unhurried, everyday conversation
after work, occasionally a short low laugh. These voices sit deep in the distance
behind the wind, blurred by the open air: the language and the tone are audible,
but not one single word is distinct or intelligible. No voice is ever close to
the microphone and no single speaker stands out from the group. No English, no
shouting, no calling out, no singing.
One horse breathes out and shifts its hooves once, also far away at the camp.
The two people in the foreground are completely silent for the whole take.

FRAME LAW: the framing is identical in every frame of the take; any reframe,
push, pan, tilt or drift = failed take.
SCALE LAW: both seated people stay exactly the size they are in the attached
frame, small and distant, roughly one twentieth of the frame height; either of
them rendered larger or closer than in the attached frame = failed take.
MOVEMENT LAW: something visibly moves in every second of the take — the smoke and
the firelight continuously, the grass as a slow travelling wave, the chapan hem
and the breathing. A frozen, photographic moment anywhere in the take = failed
take.
GRASS LAW: the grass bends as a soft continuous wave and every blade keeps its
shape from frame to frame; grass dissolving into shimmer, warble or synthetic
pattern = failed take.
STILLNESS LAW: both seated people remain seated, side by side, facing the same
way, for the whole take; neither stands, walks, turns toward the other, gestures,
or lies down. A head turning toward the other person = failed take.
MOUTH LAW: neither of the two seated people speaks or moves their mouth at any
point; every audible voice belongs to the distant camp at frame-left and to
nobody else.
DISTANCE LAW: the voices stay far away and blurred behind the wind; the wind is
always louder than the voices. A clearly intelligible word, a close-miked voice,
or a voice louder than the wind = failed take.
HEIGHT LAW: the man in the pale chapan is the larger of the two, his head clearly
higher in frame; the two heads are never the same height.
COUNT LAW: exactly two people seated apart at frame-centre, and the group by the
fire keeps the number it has in the attached frame; no one walks into frame and
no one leaves it. Any additional person or horse = failed take.
Nothing modern appears anywhere in frame.

PHYSICS — HORSES, ALL THREE SHOTS
Every horse runs at a full gallop with a complete real stride: the hind legs land
and drive, the forelegs reach forward, and there is one clear moment of suspension
per stride when all four hooves are off the ground. Each hoof reaches forward,
strikes the turf, takes the full weight of the animal, compresses the fetlock and
drives back off the ground. Each horse has exactly four correctly jointed legs and
one head in every frame. Every rider stays mounted and upright, weight carried
through the stirrups, moving with the horse.
